name: Young Circle baobab (south end)

location.address: ArtsPark at Young Circle, 1 Young Circle, Hollywood, FL 33020

access: Free. ArtsPark at Young Circle is a city park open 7:00 AM to 11:00 PM daily (City of Hollywood page); ADA accessible, street parking.
verify_notes: Register: Florida Champion (Broward), circumference 416 in = 1057 cm, height 55 ft = 16.8 m, crown 78x74 ft, measured 2016-02-22 (register date field 1456099200000). Register location text: south end of the park. City of Hollywood page says the park is 'one of the few places in the United States where you can see five Baobab Trees' and calls baobabs 'the second widest species of tree in the world'. Planting date and planter undocumented: nursery page says locally believed 1930s-1940s; monumentaltrees.com (cross-check only) reasons ~1926 from a 1935 photo of the circle (then Harding Circle); a Substack blog argues far older from African growth rates, a blog inference, not used. Do not state an age. Dispute noted, no source names a planter, nothing links J. W. Young. A fountain in the park (Millennium Springs, Ritsuko Taho) is tied to the energy waves of one baobab (search snippet, not fetched; leave out unless seen). Pin = register coordinate in the park, not shown to land on one crown, so approximate. Sits ~115 m from ftl_006 (the park's other registered baobab); both could be told as one stop at Young Circle. Alive: city page current, register measured 2016, lifecheck NONE; 'flagged' thin alive evidence, no dated recent photo seen. One source plus city page (US bar met).
story:
The biggest baobab in Florida grows in the middle of a traffic circle. When the Florida Forest Service measured it in February 2016, the trunk was 10.57 metres round, the tree 16.8 metres tall and its crown about 24 metres across, enough to make it the state champion of its species.

Young Circle is the roundabout at the centre of downtown Hollywood, and its middle is a city park now, ArtsPark. The City of Hollywood says the park is one of the few places in the United States where you can see five baobabs, an African species it calls the second widest kind of tree in the world. The state register lists two of them. This one stands at the south end. The other, a challenger 8.64 metres round, stands on the west side, about 115 metres away, and the two make one easy stop.

When this tree went in, and who planted it, nobody has written down. Local accounts place it in the 1930s or 1940s. Some writers argue for something far older, reasoning from how slowly baobabs grow in Africa. Neither claim rests on a planting record, so we give no age.

The measurement is from 2016, and the city still names its baobabs as a reason to visit the park. Entry is free. If you have stood under it lately, or know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, more than ten metres round, the widest of the registered pair. It stands at the south end of ArtsPark; the other registered baobab is on the west side, about 115 metres away.

story:
Florida's champion baobab is not the taller of the two the state measured in its own park. Its neighbour on the west side of Young Circle tops it by 30 centimetres, at 17.1 metres, measured four days later in February 2016.

The state register files this one as a Florida Challenger, a tree close enough to the champion on points to be in contention. The difference is in the trunk. This one measured 8.64 metres round, the champion at the south end of the park 10.57, and girth counts most in the register's sum. Its crown spread about 23 metres one way and 20 the other.

Both stand in ArtsPark, the city park that fills the middle of the Young Circle roundabout in downtown Hollywood, about 115 metres apart. The City of Hollywood says five baobabs grow there, which makes the park one of the few places in the United States to see that many together. Only two are on the state register, so the other three are there for anyone who wants to pace them out.

No record says when these trees were planted. Local accounts guess the 1930s or 1940s, and others argue for far older, but nobody has produced a date, so we leave the age empty. The park is free and open from early morning until late evening. If you know the story of how baobabs came to a Hollywood traffic circle, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the taller, narrower of the two registered baobabs, 8.64 metres round. It stands on the west side of ArtsPark at Young Circle, about 115 metres from the champion at the south end.

story:
This mahogany is wider than it is tall. Its crown spreads 38 metres one way and 33 the other over a tree that stands 28 metres high, and it grows next to the restrooms of a suburban park in Plantation.

The Florida Forest Service measured it in June 2024 and lists it as the state champion of its species: 4.17 metres round the trunk, 28 metres tall, and a crown that covers more ground than the tree has height. The register scores a tree on its girth, its height and a quarter of its average crown spread, so here the spread does real work in the sum.

African mahogany is native to West Africa, and this one was planted here, an ocean away from its range. Nobody has published when. The register gives no planting date and neither does the park's own page, so the tree has no age here. A trunk of just over four metres says something about size, not years.

The measurement is recent, which matters in hurricane country. As of June 2024 this one was standing and spreading.

Plantation Woods is a free city park, open from eight in the morning until dusk and closed on Wednesday mornings. No ticket, no tour, only a walk to the restrooms and a look up. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, about 38 metres across and wider than the tree is tall. It stands next to the restrooms in Plantation Woods Park.

Register spelling 'Hurea crepitans' is Hura crepitans; Wikipedia's Flamingo Gardens page lists a 'dynamite tree' in the arboretum, which links to the Sandbox tree article (the species is known for explosive seed pods, from general knowledge, add a source before use). Flamingo Gardens already holds four published trees (the Earpod Tree etc.); this is a different trunk. Approximate pin on register coordinate. Alive: measured 2024. Owner is Flamingo Gardens; Wikipedia says 23 champion trees.
story:
Flamingo Gardens grows Florida's biggest sandbox tree and, about 570 metres away across the same garden, one of the trees chasing it. This is the chaser.

The Florida Forest Service measured it in August 2024 at 3.35 metres round and 26.8 metres tall, with a crown about 22 metres across, and lists it as a Florida Challenger. The champion stands on the west side of the children's garden, 4.04 metres round and above 30 metres high. Two trees of one species on the state register, inside one ticketed garden, says a good deal about the place.

Flamingo Gardens began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and grew into a botanical garden and wildlife sanctuary in Davie, west of Fort Lauderdale. Wikipedia counts 23 Florida champion trees on its grounds, and its list includes a dynamite tree, the other common name of this species. The register places this one in the rainforest ridge area.

Nobody has recorded when it was planted, and nothing ties this trunk to the 1927 homestead, so its age stays blank. Entry to the garden is paid. If you are going for the champion anyway, this one is a short walk on, and makes the pair worth comparing. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the smaller of the garden's two registered sandbox trees, 3.35 metres round and 26.8 metres tall. It stands in the rainforest ridge area; the champion is by the children's garden.

Register location text is only 'Flamingo gardens'; coordinate is the register's. A girth of 3 m on a gumbo limbo is large for the species (its smooth red peeling bark is the species' trait, general knowledge). Approximate pin. Alive: measured 2024.
story:
Among the imported giants of Flamingo Gardens, this one is a local. The gumbo limbo is native to South Florida, and this trunk measured 3.05 metres round in August 2024, a girth that is big for its species.

The Florida Forest Service lists it as a Florida Challenger, a tree in contention for the state title. It is not tall. At 13.7 metres it is the shortest of the garden's trees on this list, about half the height of the sandbox and candlenut trees nearby, and its crown, roughly 15 metres by 11, spreads less than theirs too. What earns it a place on the register is the trunk.

The garden around it began as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and is now a botanical garden and wildlife sanctuary in Davie, west of Fort Lauderdale, with 23 Florida champion trees by Wikipedia's count. The garden's other record-holders on our map came from elsewhere in the tropics. The gumbo limbo is the one that belongs to this part of Florida.

The register says only that it stands at Flamingo Gardens and gives a coordinate, so our pin is approximate. Look for a short, thick trunk near that point. No one has recorded when it was planted, or whether it was planted at all, so we give no age. Entry is paid. If you can tell us more, please do.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by a short, thick trunk, 3.05 metres round on a tree only 13.7 metres tall. It stands near our approximate pin inside Flamingo Gardens.

name: Flamingo Gardens candlenut tree

location.address: Flamingo Gardens, 3750 S Flamingo Rd, Davie, FL 33330

official_register.name: Florida Forest Service Champion Tree Register

access: Paid entry to Flamingo Gardens (see ftl_008). Open daily 9:30 AM to 5 PM. Stands in the tropical rainforest area, which a narrated tram ride passes (Wikipedia).
verify_notes: Register: Florida Champion, circumference 90 in = 229 cm, height 80 ft = 24.4 m, crown 43x59 ft, measured 2024-08-27. Register location text: tropical rainforest area of Flamingo Gardens. Approximate pin on register coordinate. Alive: measured 2024.
story:
Florida's biggest candlenut tree is built like a mast. It rises 24.4 metres on a trunk only 2.29 metres round, and the Florida Forest Service, measuring it in August 2024, ranked it the state champion of its species.

The crown is narrow for that height and uneven, about 13 metres one way and 18 the other. It stands in the tropical rainforest area of Flamingo Gardens in Davie, the stretch of the garden that the narrated tram ride passes through, so you can see it from a seat as well as on foot.

Flamingo Gardens started as the Wray family's homestead in 1927 and now holds 23 Florida champion trees, by Wikipedia's count. Three registered trees stand within a short walk in this part of the garden. Besides this candlenut there is a challenger sandbox tree about 120 metres off and a thick-trunked gumbo limbo a little further. The garden's other champions, the earpod and the dynamite tree among them, stand a few hundred metres west.

No one has recorded when this tree was planted, so it has no age on our page. A slim trunk on a tall tree says nothing either way. Entry to the garden is paid. If you know its planting date, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height on a slim trunk, 24.4 metres tall and only 2.29 metres round. It stands in the tropical rainforest area of Flamingo Gardens, which the tram ride passes.
